solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Girl abruptly turned, fibbed and rushed out

indicators.note: something ended abruptly is cut short, so the word loses its final letter
turning something round makes it face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a lass is a girl
to fib is to tell a lie

explanation.surface: A girl spins round, tells a lie and storms out of the room.
explanation.walkthrough: LASS cut short is LAS, which turned gives SAL; that plus LIED makes SALLIED.
explanation.definitionFit: To sally is to make a sudden charge or excursion out, so the past tense matches dashing outside.

clue.text: Layers of deposits and hair in sewer

blocks.note: a seam is a layer of coal or ore in rock
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: Grimy sludge and hair clogging an underground drainage pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' looks like the drain; read it as one who sews. SEAMS and TRESS give SEAMSTRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who stitches clothes for a living is literally one who sews, hence a sewer.

clue.text: Not at all tight, WC Fields rose at last

indicators.note: at last points to the final position, so only the closing letter of each word counts

blocks.note: a WC (water closet) is a loo, British slang for a toilet
the final letters of these two words

explanation.surface: The comedian W.C. Fields, sober for once, got up late.
explanation.walkthrough: W.C. Fields was a famously boozy American comic, which makes 'tight' (drunk) apt; here WC is just a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Something slack, with no tension or grip, is the opposite of tight in the physical sense.

clue.text: Rude about Victor having no money

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps round the other

blocks.note: insolent means rude and disrespectful
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is rude about Victor, who is broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rude about Victor' reads as gossip; 'about' is the instruction to wrap one word round the letter for Victor.
explanation.definitionFit: A person or firm unable to pay debts is bankrupt, the formal term for lacking funds.

clue.text: My dear Dotty is away with the fairies

indicators.note: dotty means crazy or scatty, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fond remark that a dear woman named Dotty is in a world of her own.
explanation.walkthrough: Dotty looks like a name, capitalised as it starts the clue's second part; it is the anagram signal. 'Away with the fairies' is a British idiom for being vague and absent-minded.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lost in daydreams, vague and distracted, is described with this idiom for absent-mindedness.

clue.text: Poem about moon

indicators.note: about here means all around, letters scattered into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A verse written about the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moon' looks like a noun, the subject of the poem; it is a verb, to moon about.
explanation.definitionFit: To moon is to wander listlessly in a dejected way, the same as sulking aimlessly.

clue.text: Whatever starts to make everyone happy

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: the first letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Whatever you do at the start will keep everyone content.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the answer, an expression of indifference, is the opposite of making everyone happy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dismissive interjections expressing boredom or indifference, used as a shrug in speech.

clue.text: Clipped little horse, pet for pope

indicators.note: something clipped is trimmed, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: a pony is a small horse
a pet is a fit of sulking, as in 'in a pet'; a tiff is a petty quarrel

explanation.surface: A trimmed pony offered as a pet for the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like a beloved animal; here it means a fit of pique, a sulk or minor quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bishop of Rome is formally styled Supreme Pontiff, the title of the head of the Catholic Church.

clue.text: Regularly visited Bangkok in the past

indicators.note: visiting at regular intervals means calling at every other stop, so alternate letters are kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Someone used to be a frequent visitor to Bangkok years back.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the even letters of Bangkok: A, G, O.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed after a time span it means before now, so 'years before now' and 'back then' match.

clue.text: He gets in drunk and hopping mad

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about unsteadily, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man comes home drunk and furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets in' looks like a container instruction; all three words are the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Being furious inside, boiling with rage, is a figurative sense drawn from liquid bubbling hot.

clue.text: I learned an unusual response to stress

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters fall into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they discovered an odd way of coping with pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: the hormone is not the response itself but what the body releases in that response.
explanation.definitionFit: The hormone surges from the adrenal glands under fear or pressure, driving the fight-or-flight reaction.

clue.text: Voiced appropriate toughness

indicators.note: something voiced is spoken, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: to appropriate is to take for oneself, to steal

explanation.surface: Someone spoke with a firmness suited to the occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as an adjective (suitable); it is the verb meaning to take without permission.
explanation.definitionFit: The metal stands for hard resolve, as in nerves of steel, meaning mental strength.

clue.text: People may object to Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner was the Oxford don famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so initial sounds trade places

blocks.note: may and can both express being able or allowed
to mind is to object, as in 'do you mind?'
swap the opening C and M sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: A warning that the public might complain to Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the M and the hard C sounds of the two words gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Humanity taken as a whole, the human race, is what this collective noun names.

clue.text: Huge robin worried nearby resident

indicators.note: worried means agitated or shaken about, so the letters are disturbed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An enormous robin in the garden has alarmed the person living next door.
explanation.walkthrough: Note the British spelling with -OUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone living next door or close by is the person who shares your street or block.

clue.text: Essentially crass female’s a bit of a pig

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: the middle three letters
a female's is hers; her is the possessive for a woman

explanation.surface: A boorish woman is called something of a pig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a pig' sounds like an insult; read literally it is a slice of pork. A rasher is a slice of bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin slice of bacon is literally a small piece cut from the animal, hence a portion of pork.

clue.text: Leaves tots to be raised by a companion

indicators.note: in a down clue raising something lifts it from bottom to top, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: a tot or nip is a small measure of spirits
taken as written
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A parent abandons the children to be brought up by a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' and 'tots' suggest a parent walking out on small children; both are nouns here: greens, and drams of whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: The vegetable is eaten as its dark green foliage, so a dish of it is literally leaves.

clue.text: In flap, if fleeing bull

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the following words, running on unbroken

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: In a panic, as though running from a charging bull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bull' looks like the animal being fled; it is slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for nonsense or rubbish talk, the slang sense of bull being short for a cruder term.

clue.text: Naked relative scratching backside with plug

indicators.note: to scratch is to strike out, and the backside is the rear end, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: an uncle is a relative
a plug is a piece of publicity, an advertisement

explanation.surface: A nude family member scratching their bottom while holding a plug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratching backside' paints an unseemly picture; it means striking out the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Clad means clothed, so the negative form describes someone wearing no clothes, i.e. nude.

clue.text: Struck face of scoundrel with glove

indicators.note: the face is the front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: the first letter
a mitten is a kind of glove

explanation.surface: Someone slapped a villain across the face with a glove, as in a challenge to a duel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the old custom of challenging a cad to a duel; 'with' just joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Smite means to hit hard, and its past participle is an old form meaning hit or afflicted.

clue.text: Sweet prince, very sad at heart

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so the middle letter is kept

blocks.note: Prince Hal, the young Henry V in Shakespeare's plays
V is the abbreviation for very
the middle letter

explanation.surface: A charming prince who is deeply unhappy inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like an adjective describing the prince; it is the definition, a noun for a confection.
explanation.definitionFit: A Middle Eastern confection made of sesame paste and honey, it counts as a type of candy.

clue.text: Compare fungus and alga, as some might say

indicators.note: how some people say a word points to its pronunciation, not its spelling

blocks.note: a lichen is a partnership of a fungus and an alga

explanation.surface: A biology exercise asking students to contrast a fungus with an alga.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As some might say' because LICHEN is also pronounced 'litchen'; only one pronunciation matches.
explanation.definitionFit: To liken one thing to another is to point out their similarity, the same as comparing them.

clue.text: Moved to a lower station

indicators.note: letters that are moved are shifted out of place into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone has been demoted to a humbler post or a lesser rank.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one phrase meaning demoted; 'station' (rank) is really a London railway terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: London's busiest rail terminus bears the name of the 1815 battle, so it is a railway station.

clue.text: Tree found in Israel, mostly

indicators.note: found in says the letters are tucked inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A tree that grows mainly in Israel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' looks like a deletion signal for Israel; it is part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall deciduous hardwood once common in English hedgerows, it is a familiar kind of tree.

clue.text: Caught evasive fish

indicators.note: to catch a remark is to hear it, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: coy means reluctant to give details, evasive

explanation.surface: An angler lands a slippery fish that kept dodging the hook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' reads as landing a fish; here it means heard. In cricket it is C, a tempting false path.
explanation.definitionFit: These ornamental carp from Japan are kept in garden ponds, a decorative variety of fish.

clue.text: Person who feigns silence in the morning

blocks.note: sh is the call for silence
a.m. marks the morning hours

explanation.surface: Someone pretending to be quiet early in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person who feigns' looks like it wants an actor or faker; the answer is usually a thing, but it can also mean an impostor.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun can denote an impostor or pretender, one who fakes something, not just a fake thing.

clue.text: Make crazy gardener endlessly angry

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped
something angry is worked up and agitated, so the letters are thrown about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Driving a perpetually furious gardener mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angry' looks like part of the definition; it is the anagram signal for GARDENE.
explanation.definitionFit: To unhinge someone's mind is to drive them mad, which is what deranging means.
